---
title: "Coming from r5r"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("setup.R")
```

peabiru is meant as a drop-in for the routing functions of r5r 2.5.0. This
page lists what is the same, what is different on purpose, and what is not
there yet.

## The same

- **Function names, arguments and defaults** of `build_network()`,
  `travel_time_matrix()`, `accessibility()`, `expanded_travel_time_matrix()`
  and `arrival_travel_time_matrix()`. The first argument is still called
  `r5r_network`; the older name `r5r_core`, deprecated in r5r 2.3.0, is
  still accepted with a warning, as r5r does.
- **Argument checks** follow r5r's, in the same order and with the same
  bounds and conversions (a factor `mode`, a POSIXlt `arrival_datetime`), so
  an argument r5r rejects is rejected here too. The messages say the same
  thing but are not word for word r5r's (which come from cli and checkmate).
  A few calls that r5r accepts are errors here; they are listed
  [below](#differences).
- **Results**: the same rows, in the same order, with the same column names,
  types and values. For a frequency-based feed this needs the same `seed`
  (without one, both packages draw from the clock and every run differs).

A call written for r5r runs unchanged once the package is swapped, as long as
it passes a network built by `peabiru::build_network()`, uses only what is
supported, and does not rely on the result being a `data.table`. Here both
packages compute the same matrix on the sample network, and the results are
compared with `identical()`:

```{r, include = FALSE}
# r5r needs a JDK 21; site/build.sh points JAVA_HOME to one when it can.
run_r5r <- requireNamespace("r5r", quietly = TRUE) &&
  nzchar(Sys.getenv("JAVA_HOME"))
```

```{r, eval = run_r5r, message = FALSE}
options(java.parameters = "-Xmx2G")

# r5r writes its network.dat into the data directory: give it a copy
r5r_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "spo")
dir.create(r5r_dir)
invisible(file.copy(list.files(data_path, pattern = "\\.(pbf|zip)$", full.names = TRUE),
                    r5r_dir))
r5r_network <- r5r::build_network(r5r_dir, verbose = FALSE)

args <- list(origins = points, destinations = points,
             mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"), departure_datetime = departure,
             percentiles = c(25, 50, 75), seed = 42, n_threads = 2,
             progress = FALSE)
from_r5r <- do.call(r5r::travel_time_matrix, c(list(r5r_network), args))
from_peabiru <- do.call(peabiru::travel_time_matrix, c(list(network), args))

identical(as.data.frame(from_r5r), from_peabiru)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !run_r5r}
cat("*(This chunk was not run when the page was built: it needs r5r and a JDK 21.)*\n")
```

## How parity is checked {#parity}

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Parity: the same inputs go through r5r 2.5.0 (R5 7.6 on Java) and peabiru, and the outputs are compared for exact equality: matrices pair by pair, accessibility bit for bit, expanded and arrival matrices column by column and in order, and data frames with identical() in R."}
fig("parity.svg")
```

The `identical()` comparison above is how parity is tested:
`bench/compare/r_parity.R` in the repository runs dozens of such comparisons
on r5r's Porto Alegre and São Paulo samples (street and transit matrices,
accessibility, expanded and arrival matrices, edge cases) and fails on any
difference.

"The same results" is meant literally: every travel time, every accessibility
value (as a double, to the last bit) and every row of the expanded and arrival
matrices, in the same order. The comparisons run on r5r's two sample cities,
Porto Alegre (timetables) and São Paulo (frequencies), with parameters chosen
to exercise the edge cases: short time windows, walking limits, every
percentile and decay function, origins that cannot be linked, trips across
midnight. The scripts are in `bench/compare/` in the repository.

This works because the engine is a port of R5 7.6, the engine r5r drives, and
follows its rules down to details that only matter on ties: the order in
which ways, feeds and stops are read, which of two equal paths is kept, how
lengths and speeds are rounded, the random number generator behind the
Monte Carlo draws (a Mersenne Twister seeded from `seed` and the origin's
coordinates, as in R5), and the exponential of the decay functions
(Apache Commons Math's `FastMath.exp`, which R5 calls, instead of the C
library's). Limits are R5's too, such as the 5,000 destinations accepted by
the expanded and arrival matrices.

Results can differ between machines when a network has more than one GTFS
feed. R5 loads the feeds in the order in which the operating system lists the
directory, and peabiru does the same; that order depends on the file system.
On r5r's Porto Alegre sample (two feeds), r5r on macOS and r5r on Linux give
the same travel-time matrices and accessibility, but 227 of the 605,460 rows
of the expanded matrix differ: another stop or route, and a total time up to
0.2 minutes apart. peabiru matches r5r row for row on each platform, so
reference outputs are only valid for the machine that produced them.

## Different on purpose

- **No Java.** There is no JVM to start, no `java.parameters` to set, no R5 jar
  to download and no `stop_r5()`.
- **Results are `data.frame`s**, not `data.table`s, so the package imports
  nothing. `data.table::setDT()` converts them if you prefer.
- **The network lives in memory only.** Nothing is written to the data
  directory (no `network.dat`), and the network object cannot be saved with
  `saveRDS()`: build it again in a new session, which is quick.
  `overwrite` and `temp_dir` are accepted and have no effect.
- **`build_network()` has `n_threads`**, used to read the `.pbf` file.
- **`verbose` and `progress` are checked but print nothing.**

```{r}
network
```

## Not supported yet {#differences}

Anything below stops with an error that says so; nothing is silently ignored.
These are the calls that r5r accepts and peabiru does not.

| r5r feature | In peabiru |
|---|---|
| `mode` with `"BICYCLE"` or `"CAR"` plus `"TRANSIT"`; `mode_egress` other than `"WALK"` | error |
| A subset of transit modes (`"BUS"`, `"RAIL"`, ...) instead of `"TRANSIT"` | error |
| Fares: `fare_structure`, `max_fare` | error |
| Scenarios: `new_carspeeds`, `carspeed_scale`, `new_lts` | error |
| `output_dir` | error |
| Elevation (a `.tif` or `.tiff` raster in the data directory with `elevation` other than `"NONE"`) | error |
| More than one `.pbf` in the data directory | error |
| Expanded and arrival matrices with a street mode alone | error |
| A network built by `r5r::build_network()` | error (build it with `peabiru::build_network()`) |

```{r, error = TRUE}
travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode = c("WALK", "BUS"),
                   departure_datetime = departure)
```

These r5r functions have no peabiru counterpart yet:
`isochrone()`, `detailed_itineraries()`, `pareto_frontier()`,
`street_network_to_sf()`, `transit_network_to_sf()`, `street_network_bbox()`,
`find_snap()`, `get_gtfs_errors()`, `check_transit_availability()` and the fare
structure helpers (`setup_fare_structure()`, `read_fare_structure()`,
`write_fare_structure()`). The r5r housekeeping functions (`download_r5()`,
`setup_r5()`, `stop_r5()`, `r5r_cache()`, `r5r_sitrep()`) are not needed.

## Expanded matrices with a street mode

r5r accepts `expanded_travel_time_matrix()` with a street mode alone, but
then reports the same trip for every minute of a departure time taken from
the computer's clock (`Sys.time()`), not from `departure_datetime`. peabiru
does not reproduce that and stops with an error; use `travel_time_matrix()`
for street modes.
